title: Christmas Gift Guide 2026: Tech Gifts From £5.49, Sorted by Budget and Person | Megastore76
metaDescription: Twenty-two tech gifts from £5.49 to £465.99, sorted by budget and by who you are buying for. Every price checked against the store on 29 September 2026, and every picture we show checked for claims the store cannot support.
h1: Twenty-two tech gifts, sorted by what you want to spend
intro: Christmas tech shopping goes wrong in one of two ways: spending too much on someone who wanted something small, or spending too little on someone who will use it every day. This page is the same list twice — once sorted by budget, once sorted by who you are buying for — so you can start from whichever end you already know. Every price here was checked against the store today, and every picture we show was looked at for a claim the store cannot support — a price that contradicts the checkout, or a rating, award or review count, when the store has none. Four listings failed that check and appear below without a picture.

verdict.kicker: If you only read one thing
verdict.heading: Three gifts that work for almost anyone
verdict.intro: Each of these is the safest choice in its price band — the kind of present that does not require knowing anything about the person's existing setup, phone brand or taste. If you are buying for someone you do not know well, start here.

picks.label: Under £25
picks.name: Lenovo LE209 Wireless Earbuds
picks.why: Earbuds are the most reliable gift in tech because almost everyone uses them and almost nobody objects to a spare pair. At £10.48 they are cheap enough to give as a stocking filler or to a colleague, and good enough that they will not end up in a drawer. They pair with any phone, need no setup, and there is no brand loyalty to get wrong — which is more than can be said for most tech under £25.
points: Pairs with any phone, Android or iPhone
A picture that prints no invented rating or review count
Nothing to configure and no account to create

picks.label: Around £70 — the best all-round gift
picks.name: Philips Hue Starter Kit
picks.why: This is the gift that gets used every single day, and it is the one people are least likely to have bought themselves. Smart bulbs go in the existing lamps and ceiling fittings, so there is nothing to install and nothing to replace — and unlike most tech gifts, the person sees it working the moment they switch a light on. £67.85 is the price band where a gift stops being a token and starts being something they would have bought.
points: Fits existing lamps and fittings — no rewiring
Used every day, not just at first
The effect is visible immediately, which makes it a good gift to watch opened
A picture that prints no invented rating or review count

picks.label: The showstopper
picks.name: reMarkable 2 Paper Tablet
picks.why: When the budget is genuinely large, the risk is buying something impressive that never gets used. The reMarkable 2 is the opposite: an E Ink tablet that writes like paper, for someone who takes notes, annotates documents or sketches. It is a gift for a specific kind of person — a student, a planner, someone who fills notebooks — and for that person it replaces a shelf of stationery. For anyone else it would sit unused, so buy it only if you know they write.

dives.heading: The three that need explaining
dives.intro: The rest of the list is self-explanatory. These three are the ones where a sentence of context changes whether they are the right gift.

products.name: Philips Hue Starter Kit
products.summary: A gift has to clear two bars to be worth giving: the person has to want it, and they have to not have already bought it. Smart lighting is unusually good at both — almost everyone would enjoy it, and almost nobody has got round to buying it for themselves. Hue bulbs go into existing lamps and ceiling fittings, so there is nothing to install and nothing to replace, and the person sees it work the first time they flick a switch. That immediate, visible payoff is what makes this a better gift than a gadget they have to set up and learn.

Controllable by app and voice assistant
Picture prints no invented rating or review count
pros: Used every day rather than for a week
Fits what the person already owns — no compatibility gamble
Visible immediately when opened, which makes it a good gift to watch
Philips Hue is the best-known name in smart lighting, so it is not a risky brand to give
cons: £67.85 is real money if the person turns out not to care about lighting
Smart bulbs are more expensive to replace than ordinary ones when they eventually fail
It needs a phone app to do anything beyond working as a normal bulb
If they already own Hue, this adds to a system they have rather than surprising them
products.forWho: Someone who is difficult to buy for because they already seem to have everything. Smart lighting is the category most people have not got round to.

products.name: reMarkable 2 Paper Tablet
products.summary: The danger with a large-budget gift is that it impresses on Christmas morning and then lives in a drawer. The reMarkable 2 avoids that only if you are buying for the right person: someone who takes notes by hand, annotates documents or sketches, and gets through notebooks. For that person it replaces a shelf of stationery, and the E Ink screen is genuinely paper-like rather than a tablet pretending. For anyone else — someone who takes notes on their phone, or does not take notes at all — it is an expensive object with one job. Buy it because you know they write.

Replaces paper notebooks rather than supplementing them

For a note-taker it genuinely replaces a shelf of notebooks

products.forWho: A student, planner or designer who fills notebooks and would rather not carry them. Not a general-purpose gadget.

products.name: Tuya Smart WiFi UK Plug
products.summary: Most cheap tech gifts are novelties — a gadget that gets used twice and then lives in a drawer. This is the exception. £5.49 buys a UK plug that turns any lamp, fan or heater into something you can control from your phone or by voice, and it monitors what the appliance costs to run. In January, when the novelty of most cheap gifts has worn off, this one is still doing a job. It is also the safest possible gift because it needs no account, no hub and no compatibility with anything the person already owns.

products.forWho: The person who is hard to buy for because they buy themselves everything they want. A cheap gift that does a real job beats an expensive one that does not.

guide.heading: Four things to get right before December
guide.intro: The gifts are the easy part. This is the part that decides whether they arrive.

points.h: Buy in early December, not mid-December
points.p: Every gift here is posted, and the last week before Christmas is when delivery times stop being reliable for anything, including tracked services. Ordering in the first week of December costs you nothing and removes the single most common way a good gift becomes a disappointment. If you are buying after about the 18th, assume it may not arrive.

points.h: Check the price before you assume Black Friday beat it
points.p: Black Friday is late November and the sales run into December, so you may well get a better price by waiting. But prices on this page and in the store move, and a discount on a product that then sells out is not a saving. Check the store page for the current price rather than trusting a figure you saw a fortnight ago — every price on this page carries the date it was checked.

points.h: Match the gift to their phone and their room, not to the spec
points.p: This is where tech gifts go wrong. An Apple Watch will not pair with an Android phone. A robot vacuum that suits a flat will struggle in a three-storey house. A smart plug is useless for ceiling lights. Every item above names who it suits — read that line before the specification, because the specification is what makes a gift look good in the listing and the match is what makes it get used.

points.h: Spend the middle, not the extremes
points.p: The two riskiest price bands are the cheapest and the most expensive. Very cheap tech gifts are usually novelties that get used twice, and very expensive ones are usually bought on a guess about what someone wants. The £30 to £80 band — the Hue kit, the Echo Dot, the gaming headsets, the doorbell — is where a gift is substantial enough to be used daily and cheap enough that being slightly wrong does not matter.

proof.heading: Three things worth knowing
proof.intro: Including one about the store itself, which is why this list is shorter than the catalogue.

cards.b: The pictures are checked, not just the prices
cards.p: Most listings in this store use a seller-made marketing graphic rather than a photograph of the item, and a few of those graphics print a price the store does not charge or a rating it has never earned. So we looked at the picture on every gift here. Four carried a claim the store cannot support, or showed a different product from the one on the listing, and they appear on this page without a picture rather than with a misleading one. The rest are the listings’ own images, and you should read them as illustrations of the model, not photographs of the box that arrives.

cards.b: Nothing here needs the person's existing setup
cards.p: Every gift above works on its own or with any phone. There is nothing here that requires knowing which brand they already own, or buying a companion accessory — the two ways a well-meant tech gift ends up unusable.

cards.b: We are the seller, not an independent reviewer
cards.p: Megastore76 sells every product on this page, so this is a shop's own gift guide. The drawbacks listed against each pick are real ones, including where they make a product a worse gift than the headline price suggests.

faq.q: When should I start Christmas tech shopping in 2026?
faq.a: The first week of December. Every gift on this page is posted, and the final week before Christmas is when delivery becomes unreliable regardless of which service is used. Buying in early December costs nothing extra and avoids the most common way a good gift turns into an apology. If you are ordering after about the 18th, assume it may not arrive in time.

faq.q: What is the best last-minute tech gift?
faq.a: A digital product, because there is nothing to post. The Megastore76 Ministry Suite at £147 is delivered as a download, so it can be bought and given on Christmas Eve. Among physical gifts, the smart plugs and earbuds under £25 are the ones most likely to still be in stock late.

faq.q: Are Black Friday deals better than the Christmas sales?
faq.a: Usually yes for electronics, but it depends on the product, and the risk is stock rather than price — a discount on something that then sells out is not a saving. Check the current price on the store page rather than trusting a figure you saw earlier, because prices move. Every price on this page records the date it was checked.

faq.q: How do I choose a tech gift for someone I do not know well?
faq.a: Stick to things that work with any phone and need no setup: earbuds, a smart plug, a Bluetooth speaker, or the Philips Hue starter kit if the budget stretches. Avoid anything that depends on their phone brand — an Apple Watch will not pair with Android, and a Galaxy Watch will not pair with an iPhone. Every item on this page names who it suits.

faq.q: Why are there only twenty-two gifts here?
faq.a: Because we wanted a list we could stand behind rather than the whole catalogue. Every price here was checked against the store, and every picture was checked for a claim the store cannot support. Four gifts failed the picture check — the KVIDIO headphones and the WiFi Smart Plug 4-Pack, whose images print a price or a rating the store cannot honour, and two whose pictures show a different product from the one on the listing: the robot vacuum, pictured as another brand’s machine, and the Oura Ring 4, pictured as an unbranded ring bearing none of the Oura’s identifying design. They are still on the page and still priced; they simply have no picture. We would rather show you twenty-two with honest images than two hundred where the pictures are not the products.

faq.q: Is a robot vacuum a good Christmas gift?
faq.a: For the right home. The Compact Robot Vacuum at £149.99 suits a flat or a single floor; it will struggle in a three-storey house, and it is not a replacement for a full-sized vacuum for stairs and deep cleaning. As a gift it works best for someone who has said, out loud, that they hate hoovering.

faq.q: What if I do not know their existing tech?
faq.a: Buy something that does not interact with it. Earbuds, a smart plug, a lapel microphone, a games controller — all of these work independently of whatever phone or computer the person already has. The gifts to avoid when you do not know are smartwatches, which are tied to a phone brand, and anything that needs a specific hub.
